newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia sees rising world dairy prices.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia sees rising world dairy prices.

text.p: World dairy prices look set to improve in 1997, but with variations from product to product, the Australian Dairy Corp (ADC) said in its Dairy Moves.
European Union (EU) and U.S. domestic and export subsidies would still have a major impact on world dairy prices, ADC general manager planning and information Chris Phillips said.

Limits to the impact on prices of EU subsidised exports would be set by budgetary pressures and the Uruguay Round, he said. The U.S. faced similar constraints, although an expected fall in U.S. domestic prices could lead to additional pressure for subsidised exports in the first half of the year, it said.
Underlying demand for dairy products from emerging Asian markets remained firm, although slowing economic growth could cause easing import growth in 1997, Phillips said.
The short-term outlook for butterfat was uncertain, with Russian demand a key key, he said.
Lower prices should help boost Asian demand, in turn stabilising prices and maintaining export volumes, he said.
Stronger Asian demand was expected for cheese.
The EU and U.S. would offer modest increases in access opportunities because of the Uruguay Round, he said.
Continuing slow economic growth in Japan, together with continued weakness of the yen, may dampen short-term market opportunities there, Phillips said.
It was unlikely that 1997 prices would regain the peaks of late 1995/early 19956, he said.

International milk powder prices should stabilise in a US$1,800-$2,000 a tonne range, he said. Butterfat prices were likely to be more volatile in a $1,400-$1,500 a tonne range. Cheese prices were expected to be relatively stable, with prices of more than $2,000 a tonne for bulk cheddar.
